report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: The Effect of an ADHD Diagnostic Label: Stigmatizing or Protective?

author.affiliation: University of Western Ontario • Ronald V. Auguste -University of Western Ontario • Marilyn Chege -University of Western Ontario • J. Bruce Morton -University of Western Ontario • Ryan Stevenson -University of Western Ontario

text.text: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by clinical symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity.

These symptoms are often accompanied by social stigmatization, including negative descriptors, animalistic characterizations, emotional reactions of anger, and desired social distance from individuals with ADHD.
Stigmatization can negatively impact diagnosis, treatment, and behavioural functioning.
This study investigates how diagnostic labels and the gender of individuals with ADHD influence stigma-related responses.
Specifically, it examines whether the presence of an ADHD diagnostic label reduces or exacerbates stigma and how gender affects these perceptions.
Utilizing a 2x3 factorial design, participants were presented with vignettes describing a 12-year-old child with ADHD behaviours.
These vignettes varied by diagnostic label (Label vs No Label) and gender (Female, Male, and Gender-Neutral).
Stigma was assessed through four outcome variables: positive-negative attitudes, humanistic-animalistic attitudes, emotional reactions, and social distance.
Findings indicate that the presence of a diagnostic label significantly reduced negative attitudes, anger, and social distance.
Gender effects were observed but were not statistically significant.
Notably, the female vignette condition showed the strongest trends, suggesting that a diagnostic label may be particularly beneficial for females, who often go underdiagnosed.
These findings highlight the potential of diagnostic labels to reduce stigma and promote social acceptance.
The Effect of an ADHD Diagnostic Label: Stigmatizing or Protective?

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that is characterized by clinical symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity (American Psychological Association [APA], 2013).
text.formatted: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that is characterized by clinical symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity (American Psychological Association <ref type="bibr">[APA], 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Typical manifestations of inattention include difficulty concentrating, disorganization, and forgetfulness (American Psychological Association [APA], 2013).
Hyperactivity and impulsivity are often expressed through excessive talking, fidgeting, and a tendency to become easily frustrated.
ADHD has an approximate worldwide prevalence rate of 5-9% of children and 3-5% of adults, making it one of the most widespread and debilitating childhood disorders.
In Canada, approximately 1 in 21 individuals, or about 1.8 million Canadians, have ADHD (CAMH, 2024).
text.formatted: In Canada, approximately 1 in 21 individuals, or about 1.8 million Canadians, have ADHD <ref type="bibr">(CAMH, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: According to the Diagnostic Statistic Manual (DSM-5), an ADHD diagnosis requires that symptoms are exhibited across multiple contexts, such as home, school or work, and social settings, leading to significant challenges in many facets of an individual's life (American Psychological Association [APA], 2013).
Despite ADHD's high prevalence, diagnosis rates are three to four times more common in males than females (CADDAC, 2024).
text.formatted: Despite ADHD's high prevalence, diagnosis rates are three to four times more common in males than females <ref type="bibr">(CADDAC, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Females with ADHD are more likely to present predominantly inattentive symptoms, contributing to the underdiagnosis and misperception of ADHD in females (Rucklidge, 2008).

text.text: This disparity points to the influence of societal and clinical biases in identifying ADHD across genders.
Examining how ADHD is perceived across genders may reveal biases that impact diagnosis and treatment.
For individuals with ADHD, navigating a world that often misunderstands their behaviour and labels them as "troublemakers" can feel isolating and disheartening (Wilens & Spencer, 2010).
text.formatted: For individuals with ADHD, navigating a world that often misunderstands their behaviour and labels them as "troublemakers" can feel isolating and disheartening <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Wilens & Spencer, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Living with ADHD often entails facing different perceptions from others due to the disorder's symptoms, frequently leading to associated social stigma and isolation. Goffman (1963) defined stigma as a social identity that is devalued within a given social context.

text.text: In ADHD, common stigmatizing characterizations include negative descriptors such as "foolish," "moody," or "pessimistic," and even animalistic terms like "wild" or "untamed" (Meza et al., 2019).

text.text: These characteristics can evoke emotional reactions of anger in others and contribute to desired social distance from individuals with ADHD (Mueller et al., 2012).

text.text: Such reactions affect the experiences and self-perception of those impacted, often leading to cognitive and social impairments, observed through broader social adjustment issues, fewer acquaintances, and relationship challenges (Godfrey et al., 2021).

text.text: Given how they are perceived, the social lives of individuals with ADHD often differ from individuals without ADHD.
These perceptions can be shaped by their ADHD-related behaviours, the diagnostic label itself, or a combination of both (Law et al., 2007).

text.text: While psychiatric labels, particularly for children, raise concerns about amplifying stigma, they can also validate experiences, enable treatment access, and provide relief (Ohan et al., 2011).

text.text: Existing literature remains inconclusive on whether an ADHD diagnostic label provides protective benefits or exacerbates stigma, with studies showing mixed results (Werkhoven et al., 2022; Law et al., 2007; Hoza et al., 2005).

text.text: This study investigates three factors that may contribute to the stigmatization of ADHD: ADHD-related behaviours, the diagnostic label, and the impact of gender on these perceptions.
Specifically, it will aim to determine whether ADHD behaviours, alone or in conjunction with a diagnostic label, reduce or exacerbate stigma and how the child's gender influences peer perceptions.
Prior to presenting my study methods, this paper will first provide a general overview of stigmatization and the role of diagnostic labels in ADHD.
Following this, I will examine previous empirical findings on how diagnostic labels may contribute to or alleviate stigma.
Finally, I will analyze how these effects may vary based on gender.
Understanding these dynamics may help identify specific contributors to stigmatization and inform approaches to lessen its impact on individuals with ADHD.
Stigmatization is a pervasive barrier to mental health care, with significant implications for individuals with ADHD.
The World Health Organization describes the stigma of mental health disorders as "the most important barrier" to accessing mental health care (WHO, 2001, p. 98).

text.text: In the context of ADHD, stigma is often underestimated as a risk factor but has far-reaching effects, influencing treatment adherence, severity of symptoms, life satisfaction, and overall well-being (Mueller et al., 2012).

text.text: A recent study highlights how stigmatization deters families from pursuing necessary support for ADHD (Schoeman & Voges, 2022).

text.text: These findings stress the impact of stigmatization by highlighting how perceptions of ADHD can shape access to care and, ultimately, the well-being of individuals with the disorder.
One critical factor in these perceptions is the role of diagnostic labels.

In therapeutic settings, diagnostic labels can facilitate patients' self-understanding and help shape treatment plans by turning complex behavioural issues into defined recognizable traits (Werkhoven et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In therapeutic settings, diagnostic labels can facilitate patients' self-understanding and help shape treatment plans by turning complex behavioural issues into defined recognizable traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Werkhoven et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, Werkhoven and colleagues pointed out that labels can also be misused or overly reductionistic to the individual by interpreting all aspects of their behaviour through the lens of the diagnosis.

Beyond a therapeutic context, diagnostic labels play a role in society by streamlining communication about specific behavioural needs or enabling individuals to access accommodations more readily without repeatedly explaining their condition (Werkhoven et al., 2022).

text.text: That said, the effectiveness of diagnostic labels depends on a shared societal understanding.
Labels can also contribute to ADHD-related stigmatization by framing certain behaviours as negative social identities or reinforcing stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination.
In this way, they may perpetuate harmful assumptions and social exclusion.
Alternatively, labels may help reduce stigma by reshaping perceptions (Werkhoven et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Alternatively, labels may help reduce stigma by reshaping perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Werkhoven et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, knowing a child has an ADHD diagnosis may encourage a more empathetic response.
Considering the mixed impact of diagnostic labels, it is crucial to examine whether they ultimately serve a protective function or contribute to stigmatization.
The existing literature demonstrates these conflicting perspectives on how society perceives and interprets diagnostic labels.
For instance, a study by Hoza et al. (2005) investigated how children with ADHD are perceived by their peers and the effects on their social experiences.

text.text: The study included 165 children with ADHD (130 boys and 35 girls) and 1,298 classmates who served as peer raters.

Peer evaluations involved positive (e.g., best friends) nominations, negative (e.g., avoid as a friend) nominations, and a 5-point "liking" scale to identify key measures such as social preference, social impact, and reciprocated friendships (Hoza et al., 2005).

study relied solely on a male vignette, it leaves the influence of gender on ADHD-related stigma unexamined.
This is a crucial gap, as societal perceptions of ADHD symptoms and diagnostic labels may differ between genders.
Although many studies have investigated the psychological and social impact of ADHD, few studies have examined gender as a moderating factor.

text.text: In this quasi-replication, the primary research question is: Does ADHD behaviours, gender, or labelling an individual with ADHD reduce or exacerbate stigmatization?

Specifically, the study investigated whether a diagnostic label influences participants' perceptions of ADHD behaviours and how the gender of a child characterized in a vignette may modify these perceptions.
This study directly tested whether behaviours that are characteristic of ADHD elicit increased or reduced stigmatization when accompanied by a diagnostic label.
Social distance, a widely recognized measure of social stigma and prejudice (Wark & Galliher, 2007), was used to assess participants' attitudes.

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned to read one of these vignettes that described a child with ADHD behaviours and varied by the presence of an ADHD label (present or absent), and gender (neutral, male, or female), along with a control condition with gender-neutral descriptors and no ADHD behaviours or diagnostic label.
This design examines the potential moderating role of a diagnostic label and gender on ADHD-related stigmatization.
It is hypothesized that an ADHD diagnostic label may act as a protective factor, reducing negative evaluations and stigma-related responses.
The diagnostic label may potentially foster a greater understanding of these behaviours, thereby reducing stigmatization often associated with ADHD.
Additionally, gender as a moderator in perceptions of ADHD has not been fully explored in this context.

It is hypothesized that the gender of the character in the vignette will influence participant perceptions, with the female vignette condition expected to yield higher stigma-related responses compared to the male and gender-neutral counterparts.
Untreated ADHD can lead to significant adverse outcomes for individuals and those around them.

Given this risk, the potential benefits of receiving mental health services that accompany a diagnostic label may outweigh concerns over the potential stigmatizing effects of having a psychiatric diagnosis and may help lower barriers to care.

Participants included 717 individuals (560 females, 157 males) with mean age of 18.7 years (SD = 1.98 years) and of mixed racial and ethnic background (57.4% (n = 412) white, 15.6% (n = 112) South Asian, 20.6% (n = 148) East Asian, 4.5% (n = 32) Middle Eastern, and 1.8% (n = 13) other).

Participants were excluded from the analysis if they failed both attention checks, asking participants to recall the gender and whether a diagnostic label was stated in their vignette condition, or had more than 50% of their data missing.
Additionally, the control vignette condition was removed from the analysis to focus specifically on the effects of Diagnostic Label and Gender.
After cleaning, 574 participants (456 females, 118 males) with a mean age of 18.6 years (SD = 1.88 years) remained for the analysis.

The demographic questionnaire included 11 items assessing participants' age, sex, gender, ethnicity, country of birth, age of immigration to Canada (if applicable), socioeconomic status, education level, political views, and religiosity.
Political views were rated on a 7-point scale ranging from very liberal (1) to very conservative (7), and religiosity was also rated on a 7point scale ranging from not at all (1) to extremely (7).
Participants were randomly assigned to read one of seven vignettes adapted from Meza et al. (2019).

text.text: Six vignettes described a character named Alex with ADHD both hyperactive and inattentive ADHD behaviours.
The vignettes varied based the inclusion of an ADHD diagnostic label, and the gender of the vignette character, which was either neutral, male, or female.
A seventh vignette described a gender-neutral character with no ADHD behaviours and no diagnostic label and served as a control condition.
However, this seventh vignette condition was not included in the analysis.
The vignettes were designed to systematically examine how ADHD labels and gender influenced participants' perceptions (See Appendix D).

To measure attitudes toward the vignette character, participants rated how well they thought each of the 23 different adjectives described the character using a 7-point Likert scale, ranging from not at all (1) to extremely (7).

A series of four 2x3 factorial analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted to examine the effects of diagnostic labels (diagnostic label vs no diagnostic label) and gender (female, male, gender-neutral) on four separate outcome variables: (1) positive/negative adjectives, (2) human/animalistic adjectives, (3) emotional reaction, and (4) social distance.
Negative and animalistic adjective responses were reverse-coded to align with positive and human-related responses, respectively.
Pearson's product-moment correlation was computed to assess whether the fourth attitude-based outcome variables could be combined into a single composite score.
However, the resulting correlation coefficient (r = .48) indicated a moderate relationship, and therefore, the variables were retained as separate dependent measures.
Each of the four ANOVAs tested for the main effects of a diagnostic label, gender, and their interaction.
Assumptions of normality (assessed via the Shapiro-Wilk test) and homogeneity of variance (assessed via Levene's test) were checked for each outcome variable.
Tukey's Honest Significant Difference (HSD) tests were conducted as post hoc analyses following significant main or interaction effects for outcome variables that met the assumptions of ANOVA.
For emotional reaction and social distance, violations of these assumptions were observed.
As a result, nonparametric alternatives were used for pairwise comparisons: the Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test and the Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction.

This study examined the effects of ADHD diagnostic labels and gender on four distinct measures of stigmatization: attitudes (positive/negative and humanistic/animalistic), emotional reaction of anger, and desired social distanced.
The following section presents the results of the analyses to assess how these factors influence stigma-related responses.

Stigmatization was measured through participants' attitudes, emotional reactions, and desired social distance towards the character with ADHD behaviours.
The results confirmed that adding a diagnostic label significantly reduced negative attitudes, emotional reactions of anger, and the desire for social distance.

Specifically, participants in the Label condition showed more positive attitudes and lower levels of anger and social distance towards the vignette character, indicating that the presence of a diagnostic label led to more favourable perceptions.

While there were no significant effects of gender, the female vignette conditions exhibited the most pronounced effects, suggesting that adding a diagnostic label may have a stronger impact where ADHD behaviours are perceived as more abnormal due to the lower diagnosis rates of females.
The significant reduction in stigma-related responses in the label conditions aligns with the original hypothesis that a diagnostic label may act as a protective factor.

The presence of a diagnostic label facilitated understanding of the ADHD behaviours described, likely mitigating negative perceptions by framing these behaviours as part of a recognized disorder rather than as negative personal characteristics.
This result is consistent with the Meza et al. (2019) study, which suggests that diagnostic labels can enhance empathy and understanding, thereby reducing stigma.

text.text: One possible explanation is social desirability bias.

Dehumanizing or animalistic descriptions are extreme and socially undesirable, which may have led participants to avoid rating the character as animalistic, especially when a diagnostic label was present.
The differing results across stigma measures contribute to the conflicting findings in the literature regarding the protective effects of a diagnostic label on stigmatization.
This incongruity may, in part, be attributed to cultural differences in how ADHD and clinical diagnoses are perceived.

In cultures where ADHD is less pervasive or poorly understood, the protective effect of a diagnostic label may not be as pronounced, as it depends on a shared societal understanding (Werkhoven et al., 2022).

In the case of Canada, where the study was conducted, the observed protective effect of diagnostic labels aligns with the prevalence of clinical diagnoses.
The effect of gender was statistically non-significant.

This may be because, while the gender of the vignette character influenced the strength of the label's effect, gender congruence between the participant and character may have also shaped the results, as the participant group in this study was nearly 80% female.

ADHD in females is often underdiagnosed or manifests as the inattentive form of ADHD, which is more likely to be misunderstood, ignored, or overlooked (Rucklidge, 2008).

text.text: As a result, ADHD behaviours are often perceived as more abnormal or difficult to understand, which may explain why the addition of a diagnostic label had a larger impact on the female conditions.
This suggests that a diagnostic label could be especially crucial for females in helping others contextualize their ADHD-related behaviours, thereby reducing stigma and enhancing social acceptance.
This study has significant implications for understanding how ADHD diagnoses and the associated stigmatization influence perceptions of those with the disorder.

The findings suggest that a diagnostic label of ADHD can reduce stigma-related responses, which may help lower a barrier to receiving a diagnosis and treatment, particularly for individuals who may feel reluctant to seek it due to fear of social stigma.
This is especially important given the impact of ADHD on cognitive, social, and emotional functioning, as well as the long-term negative effects on wellbeing (Godfrey et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This is especially important given the impact of ADHD on cognitive, social, and emotional functioning, as well as the long-term negative effects on wellbeing <ref type="bibr">(Godfrey et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to the general reduction of stigma through diagnostic labelling, this study also highlights the gendered nature of ADHD perceptions.
Given that ADHD behaviours in females are often perceived as more abnormal or difficult to understand, a diagnostic label may play a crucial role in helping to normalize these behaviours.
This could encourage female-specific diagnosis and treatment of ADHD without fear of judgment.

This finding further emphasizes the need for more research into ADHD in females, which could lead to more accurate diagnosis and better-tailored interventions, helping to reduce misdiagnosis and underdiagnosis.
The following study has offered insight into the effects of diagnostic labels and gender on individuals with ADHD behaviours.
Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge some methodological limitations that may have potentially impacted the findings.
One significant limitation is the absence of a condition where the character had an ADHD label but no ADHD behaviours.
Including this condition would allow for a more precise understanding of the effects of the label alone, without the confounding influence of ADHD behaviours.
Future research should isolate the labelling effects by including this condition to clarify whether the label alone can reduce stigma.
Similarly, this study did not include a no-gender, no-label, and no-behaviour control condition within the analysis to focus exclusively on the effects of gender and label.
However, the inclusion of this condition would have provided a stronger baseline for isolating the effects of diagnosis and ADHD behaviours.
Furthermore, the current study did not account for the potential influence of gender congruence between the participant and the vignette character.

As mentioned in the Discussion of Results section, while the gender of the vignette character appeared to affect the extent of the diagnostic label's influence, it is unclear whether the observed gender effects stem from the gender of the character, the gender of the participant, or the congruency between the two.
Amplifying this limitation, the overrepresentation of female participants may have influenced the resulting gender effects and impacted the generalizability of the findings.
Future studies should aim to include a more gender-balanced sample and investigate where the gender effects truly originate.
Finally, the study sample consisted of undergraduate university students from the University of Western Ontario, while the vignette character was 12 years old.
This age gap between participants and the character may have influenced how participants perceived the character's behaviours.
The vignette descriptions used in the study were designed to mirror those of Meza et al. (2019), who described a 12-year-old child.
text.formatted: The vignette descriptions used in the study were designed to mirror those of <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Meza et al. (2019)</ref>, who described a 12-year-old child.

text.text: Future research could explore how age congruence between the participant and vignette character might impact stigma-related responses, as perceptions of ADHD may differ based on the age of both the individual being diagnosed and the individual making the judgement.
Additionally, as the participant sample was primarily Canadian, conducting this study in a different cultural context could affect how ADHD and diagnostic labels are perceived.

In sum, the present study demonstrated that the presence of a diagnostic label significantly reduced stigma-related responses towards individuals with ADHD behaviours, suggesting that labels can play an important role in mitigating negative perceptions and encouraging social acceptance.
While no significant gender effects were found, the findings highlight the potential impact of gendered perceptions of ADHD, particularly for females, who are often underdiagnosed.
Given the limitations of the current study, future research should continue to explore the role of gender congruence and cultural context in shaping stigma-related responses to ADHD diagnoses.
Understanding these dynamics is essential for improving social support and access to treatment for individuals with ADHD.
